narrative:
When the wardens came for Mara, Ilyan was already holding the key that could clear his own name. He closed his hand around it instead. Mara had seen him near the collapsed bridge, had heard the order he gave before the supports failed, and had every reason to sell that knowledge. Ilyan met her eyes across the council chamber and said, “You can keep your testimony. I’ll keep mine.” It sounded like a threat, which was useful. Fear was easier to carry when dressed as contempt.

The magistrate offered him a bargain: identify Mara as the saboteur, and the charge against him would vanish. Ilyan asked whether the magistrate intended to repair the bridge with confessions. The room laughed softly; the magistrate did not. Then Ilyan named a different price. Mara would be released to inspect the eastern supports, and he would surrender the key, his seal, and his right to speak at the inquiry. In return, the magistrate would postpone the executions until the inspection was complete.

Mara resisted first. “You don’t spend your innocence on me.”

“I’m not spending it,” he said. “I’m renting your competence.”

She understood the lie beneath the joke. He had known the supports were unsound. He had sent her across anyway because the evacuation required someone who could reach the far gate. His bargain admitted the consequence without offering the comfort of an apology. Mara took the key from his palm, but did not forgive him. At the eastern arch, she found the second break—and the warden’s false repair marks.

By dusk, her testimony had become necessary to both their survival. She returned the key, not to Ilyan, but to the magistrate’s table. “He protected me,” she said. “That doesn’t make him trustworthy.”

Ilyan inclined his head. “A promising beginning.”

The magistrate ordered them detained together until the inquiry. Mara sat beside him because the guards had chained them that way, and because, for one night, conditional trust was less dangerous than separation.
title: The Price of Silence
